summary: Kole Jain lays out how he would learn UI/UX design from scratch, ending in a 28-day plan. He first trains the design eye by pulling apart one landing page (the Superpower site) into four zones and pointing out the exact spacing, word counts and opacity that create its grouping and hierarchy. He then argues that learners should copy designs exactly rather than redesign them, shows the handful of hero layout options and says the choice depends on what the content is trying to do. He separates UI (the flavor: the same layout restyled as warm and friendly or modern and premium) from UX (the thinking behind a flow such as an onboarding that branches on team size). For a design system this gives concrete grouping and hierarchy values, a way to show one layout in two personalities as a visual sample, and a model for branching product flows [inferred].
key_ideas: Landing pages that look different often share one skeleton: main text block, navbar, stats and image.
Spacing creates grouping: the closer two elements sit, the more closely people associate them.
Short hero copy communicates fastest; the example uses seven words in the heading and 14 below.
A high-quality image makes or breaks a landing page; keep its focal point clear and its background calm.
Hierarchy can come from color and opacity, not only from font size.
To learn, copy a design exactly instead of redesigning it, so you are forced to notice the small details.
At any point there are only a handful of layout options; the right one depends on what the content is trying to do.
UI is the flavor of a design; the same layout can feel friendly or premium through styling alone.
UX (product design) is about the user's journey, not spacing or typography.
Even a simple onboarding hides many decisions, such as whether to block on email verification and whether to branch by team size.
Do not start a portfolio while learning, because your taste will start to change over the next one to two months.
The 28-day plan moves from training the eye, to cloning designs, to restyling (UI), to designing a branching flow (UX).

rules.rule: In a hero text block, put the subtext closest to the heading (8 px), the eyebrow slightly farther (12 px) and the buttons farthest (32 px).
rules.why: The spacing makes people read heading and subtext as one group, then the eyebrow, then the buttons.
rules.evidence: The subtext is only 8 pixels away

rules.rule: Keep hero copy very short, as in the example's seven-word heading and 14-word subtext.
rules.why: It communicates the message as quickly as possible.
rules.evidence: It's only seven words in the header

rules.rule: Keep the navbar small and out of the way; in the example its most prominent item is a 'Become a member' call to action [inferred].
rules.why: It stays out of your way, like most modern navs.
rules.evidence: stays out of your way just like most modern navs

rules.rule: Use a high-quality image asset on a landing page.
rules.why: The source says a high-quality asset makes or breaks most landing pages.
rules.evidence: makes or breaks most landing pages

rules.rule: Keep the hero image's focal point unobstructed: place text, nav and stats around it (in the example, above, below or to the left, leaving the center and right open).
rules.why: Everything sits around the focal point, leaving the center and right wide open for the imagery.
rules.evidence: the focal point of the image is never obstructed

rules.rule: Do not use a hero image with a busy background behind or next to the text.
rules.why: A busy image makes things a little more chaotic and the text harder to read; with one image the text on the left is basically gone.
rules.evidence: the background of the image isn't too busy

rules.rule: Create hierarchy with color as well as size: for example, set two lines at the same size and lower the secondary line's opacity.
rules.why: The lower-opacity line blends into the background and does not jump out as much.
rules.evidence: using color, not just size, to create some hierarchy

rules.rule: Choose a layout by first asking what the content is trying to do.
rules.why: All the hero layout decisions come down to that one thing.
rules.evidence: what is the content trying to do

rules.rule: For a profound statement, center the text, increase the font size and give it a lot of space.
rules.why: Layout decisions come down to what the content is trying to do, and a profound statement needs a lot of space to breathe.
rules.evidence: if you're trying to have a profound statement

rules.rule: When a features list has more items than fit on the screen, show them in a bento grid.
rules.why: The user should see all the features, and nothing is lost as they scroll down.
rules.evidence: swap this out for a bento grid

rules.rule: To make a product feel friendly and welcoming, use a warm background, colorful visuals, rounded corners and large, bubbly buttons.
rules.why: Styling changes how the same layout feels (its flavor).
rules.evidence: make this feel very friendly and welcoming

rules.rule: To make a product feel modern and professional, use much less rounded corners, less colorful and more premium imagery, and optionally add noise to the background.
rules.why: Styling changes how the same layout feels (its flavor).
rules.evidence: more modern and professional

rules.rule: Give sign-up screens an escape hatch link to the login page.
rules.why: Many people end up on the sign-up page unintentionally.
rules.evidence: escape hatch to the login page

rules.rule: Ask for team size during workspace creation and branch onboarding on it: teams get an invite-members step, individuals skip it.
rules.why: Team size is important because it shapes how the next onboarding steps function.
rules.evidence: we split into two flows

rules.rule: When learning, copy an existing design exactly instead of redesigning it, measuring details like card spacing, nav height and button padding.
rules.why: Copying forces you to notice the small details, and after a few sites the layout patterns emerge.
rules.evidence: don't redesign it. Literally copy it

rules.rule: Before designing in Figma, pull apart a site you like into its zones, spacing, text length and hierarchy.
rules.why: You start to see the decisions behind the design, and proximity, contrast, consistency and hierarchy become easier to recognise.
rules.evidence: before you ever even get into Figma

rules.rule: Do not start a portfolio while you are still learning design.
rules.why: The presenter calls it the biggest mistake a learner could make, because taste will start to change over the next one to two months.
rules.evidence: the biggest mistake that you could make

rules.rule: Keep the hero's main text block from dominating the page, and set the spacing around it intentionally.
rules.why: The source points to this as one of the design details to notice in a good landing page.
rules.evidence: doesn't dominate the page

rules.rule: In a features list, let the visuals lead and use the text only to support them.
rules.why: Layout follows what the content is trying to do, and a features list is about the visuals.
rules.evidence: the text is really just there to support the visuals

rules.rule: When learning, build a swipe file of 20 or so inspiring hero and feature sections, then annotate a couple for spacing, hierarchy and what is grouped with what.
rules.why: Week one of the plan is all about training your eye.
rules.evidence: Start by building yourself a swipe file

process.detail: Pick any site you like and break it into zones (main text block, navbar, stats, image); note spacing, word counts, what is grouped with what, and how hierarchy is made.
Week one: collect 20 or so hero and feature sections that inspire you from Mobbin, Dribbble, Pinterest or elsewhere.
Pick a couple from the swipe file and annotate spacing, hierarchy and what is grouped with what.
Pick one design you love from the swipe file and clone its hero section exactly.
Clone the feature section from the same site.
Pick a second site with a totally different layout and clone it too.
Restyle one of the layouts you built twice: once warm and friendly, once modern and premium.
Design the two screens where the onboarding journey splits: an invite-your-team page for the manager and a setup page for the solo user.
Keep focusing on the skill rather than a portfolio while your taste develops.

examples.what: Hero deconstruction of a landing page
examples.visual_note: Four zones (text block, navbar, stats, image). Subtext 8 px from the heading, eyebrow text 12 px, buttons 32 px away; seven-word heading and 14-word subtext; a small nav whose most prominent item is probably a 'Become a member' call to action [inferred]; all content sits above, below or left of the image's focal point, leaving the center and right open for imagery.

Replacing the calm hero image with a busy one makes things a little more chaotic and the text harder to read; with another image the text on the left is basically gone. A before/after for choosing hero imagery [inferred].
Two lines both at 15 px; the second at 55% opacity blends into the background, showing hierarchy through color rather than size.

The same hero shown as text left and image right, full-screen image under text, text above image, and text below image; then text centered, left-aligned or with body and CTA pushed right; then a bordered image, a full-bleed image or a slowly rotating carousel. A ready set for a visual option gallery [inferred].

examples.what: Features list turned into a bento grid
examples.visual_note: A features list that runs off the screen is rearranged into a bento grid so every feature stays visible.

One layout styled friendly (warm background, colorful visuals, round corners, large bubbly buttons) and again modern and professional (less rounded corners, less colorful premium imagery, background noise). Demonstrates that UI styling alone changes the feel.

Five screens: name and email with a link to login; email verification by link or code; workspace creation with a team-size question; then a split where teams get an invite-members screen and individuals skip it.
About 3 years ago: in-your-face, huge animations, giant text, everything moving. Now: more refined with smaller, more tasteful animations. Shows how much taste shifts.
